summary: Lists the requirements that congestion control mechanisms should meet for interactive, point-to-point real-time media such as video calls. Such traffic needs low delay and tolerates some loss, so it differs from bulk transfers and web browsing. The requirements are meant for judging candidate algorithms, particularly for WebRTC-style RTP traffic. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lists what congestion control should do for interactive calls. It prioritizes low delay while requiring media flows to share network capacity fairly.

subtitle: Requirements for congestion control that carries live, interactive media.

tldr.problem: Interactive media needs low delay and continuous delivery, while tolerating some packet loss. Congestion controls designed for bulk transfer do not necessarily meet those needs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for delay, fairness, startup, pauses, multiple streams, feedback, and queue management, then explains limitations of TCP Friendly Rate Control.
tldr.outcome: The requirements are a basis for evaluating candidate congestion controls for interactive point-to-point media. The document is Informational and specifies no algorithm.

facts.label: Delay goal
facts.value: Hundreds of milliseconds end to end

facts.label: Typical quick reaction
facts.value: A few round-trip times, likely within a second

today: RFC 8836 is an Informational IETF document published in January 2021. It provides requirements for evaluating interactive-media congestion control and is not listed as obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Interactive Media Needs Different Rules
sections.content:
Bulk transfers can wait for data to arrive reliably, and web pages can arrive in bursts. Interactive audio and video must arrive continuously within hundreds of milliseconds; late data is often useless, while some packet loss can be tolerated.

Other flows share the network, so media congestion control must work alongside TCP and other traffic. The RFC focuses on point-to-point interactive media such as RTP traffic and excludes non-interactive streaming and multicast or broadcast use.
sections.plainLanguage: In a call, data that arrives too late may no longer help. A congestion control method must keep delay low while sharing the network with other traffic.

sections.title: Delay, Fairness and Startup
sections.content:
An algorithm must aim for low delay while still giving media useful bandwidth. It must share fairly with real-time and TCP flows, and should not starve TCP when delay and bandwidth goals conflict. It should react to major path changes within a few round-trip times, likely within a second, while allowing for codec limits.

The algorithm should adapt to initial network conditions and handle large changes in offered media rate. Starting too slowly can harm the start of a conversation; starting too fast can create congestion. A useful share of bandwidth takes priority over minimum delay when those goals conflict.
sections.plainLanguage: Media should start at a useful rate, react to changes, and share capacity fairly. When low delay conflicts with enough bandwidth for useful media, the RFC gives priority to useful bandwidth.

sections.title: Pauses, Multiple Streams and Queues
sections.content:
The algorithm should remain stable when RTP streams pause or stop sending, then regain their earlier share after they resume. Where possible, it should combine information across streams that share a bottleneck and coordinate with other flows between the same endpoints.

Short bursts from web browsing or periodic video traffic should not cause the algorithm to build extra queues. It should use available signals such as packet arrival times, loss, acknowledgements, or Explicit Congestion Notification, without requiring special network support.
sections.plainLanguage: A call may pause or change its sending rate, and the congestion control should handle that without creating long queues. It should use available network feedback and coordinate related streams when possible.

sections.title: Feedback and Network Signals
sections.content:
The RFC says that Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP) will typically carry feedback for RTP streams. A suitable RTP profile should allow feedback often enough to react, while keeping feedback messages small and reducing their frequency when conditions are stable.

The algorithm should use Differentiated Services markings when available, but it cannot assume every bottleneck honors them. It should also treat an unexpected loss of feedback as a possible sign of overuse and remain stable when Active Queue Management is present.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver sends the sender short updates about the network. The updates should arrive often enough to guide the sending rate without using too much of the return path.

sections.title: Limits of Existing Methods and Security
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC) does not meet all the stated requirements. TFRC responds to loss, but not directly to delay from large buffers, and its smooth rate model does not fit media sources whose rates change in steps.

An on-path attacker could delay, delete, or insert messages and create false congestion signals. False signals that make available bandwidth seem higher could starve other flows, so algorithm designers should consider malicious on-path attackers.
sections.plainLanguage: TFRC was designed for smoother traffic and reacts mainly to packet loss, so the RFC says it does not meet the full needs of interactive media. An attacker on the path could also falsify feedback.
